'''''Prunus lusitanica''''', the '''Portuguese laurel cherry'''<ref>{{GRIN}}</ref> or '''Portugal laurel''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }}</ref><!-- not Portuguese laurel; multiple print references, e.g. Bailey, Manual of Cultivated Plants; Hillier, Manual of Trees and Shrubs.--> is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the rose [[family (botany)|family]] Rosaceae, [[native plant|native]] to the [[Iberian Peninsula]], [[Morocco]], the [[Macaronesia]]n archipelagos, and the [[French Basque Country]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Prunus lusitanica |url=http://www.floraiberica.es/floraiberica/texto/pdfs/06_087_28%20Prunus.pdf#page=20 |publisher=[[Flora Iberica]] |access-date=12 February 2024}}</ref><ref name=empp>Euro+Med Plantbase Project: [http://ww2.bgbm.org/_EuroPlusMed/PTaxonDetail.asp?NameId=29971&PTRefFk=500000 ''Prunus lusitanica''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928003623/http://ww2.bgbm.org/_EuroPlusMed/PTaxonDetail.asp?NameId=29971&PTRefFk=500000 |date=2007-09-28 }}</ref><ref name=grin>{{GRIN | accessdate = January 2, 2018}}</ref>

The split between the subspecies (subsp. ''azorica'', ''hixa'', and ''lusitanica'') is dated around the [[Pliocene]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kondraskov |first1=Paulina |last2=Schütz |first2=Nicole |last3=Schüßler |first3=Christina |last4=Sequeira |first4=Miguel Menezes de |last5=Guerra |first5=Arnoldo Santos |last6=Caujapé-Castells |first6=Juli |last7=Jaén-Molina |first7=Ruth |last8=Marrero-Rodríguez |first8=Águedo |last9=Koch |first9=Marcus A. |last10=Linder |first10=Peter |last11=Kovar-Eder |first11=Johanna |last12=Thiv |first12=Mike |title=Biogeography of Mediterranean Hotspot Biodiversity: Re-Evaluating the 'Tertiary Relict' Hypothesis of Macaronesian Laurel Forests |journal=PLOS ONE |date=14 July 2015 |volume=10 |issue=7 |article-number=e0132091 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0132091 |pmid=26173113 |pmc=4501571 |bibcode=2015PLoSO..1032091K |language=en |issn=1932-6203|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Description==
''Prunus lusitanica'' is an [[evergreen]] [[shrub]] or small [[tree]] growing to 3-8m tall (though it can reach 15-20m in cultivation).<ref name="iberica">{{cite web |title=P. lusitanica |url=http://www.floraiberica.es/floraiberica/texto/pdfs/06_087_28%20Prunus.pdf |publisher=[[Flora Iberica]] |access-date=28 January 2022}}</ref><ref name="UTAD">{{cite web |title=Prunus lusitanica subesp. lusitanica |url=https://jb.utad.pt/especie/Prunus_lusitanica_subesp_lusitanica |publisher=Jardim Botânico da UTAD |access-date=28 January 2022 |language=pt-PT}}</ref><ref name="Calouste">{{cite web |title=Azereiro |url=https://gulbenkian.pt/jardim/garden-flora/azereiro/ |publisher=[[Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation]] |access-date=28 January 2022}}</ref><ref>Hay, R. (Ed) 1978.  ''Reader's Digest Encyclopedia of Garden Plants and Flowers''. Reader's Digest Association Limited, London.</ref> The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is smooth and dark-grey.<ref name="iberica" /> The [[leaf|leaves]] are alternate, oval, 7–15 cm long and 3–5 cm broad,<ref name="iberica" /> with an acute apex and a dentate margin, glossy dark green above, lighter below.<ref name="Calouste" /> They superficially resemble those of the [[bay laurel]], which accounts for its often being mistaken for one.

The [[flower]]s are small (10–15 mm diameter) with five small white petals; they are produced on erect or spreading [[raceme]]s 15–25 cm long in late spring. The [[fruit]] is a small cherry-like [[drupe]] 8–13 mm in diameter, green or reddish green at first, turning dark purple or black when ripe in late summer or early autumn.<ref name="iberica" /><ref name=rushforth>Rushforth, K. (1999). ''Trees of Britain and Europe''. Collins {{ISBN|0-00-220013-9}}.</ref> It is edible but should not be eaten if too bitter.<ref name=pfaf/>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Hohenheim - Prunus lusitanica.jpg|thumb|right|Flowers]]
[[File:Prunus lusitanica Frutos 2010-9-26 DehesaBoyaldePuertollano.jpg|thumb|right|Ripe fruit]]
It occurs in the western [[Mediterranean Basin]], France, Spain, and Portugal, and [[Macaronesia]], Azores, Canary Islands and Madeira.

''Prunus lusitanica''  is rare in the wild, found mainly along mountain streams, preferring sunshine and moist but well-drained soils. It is moderately drought-tolerant. It reproduces either sexually (the most successful method) or asexually by cloning from shoots.<ref name=alarcon>Alarcon, J. A. C. (2001). ''Geobotany and Conservation Biology Study on Prunus lusitanica L. Iberian populations''. Departamento de Biologia. Facultad de Ciencias, Universidad Autonoma de Madrid. Available [http://bio-math10.biology.kyushu-u.ac.jp/seminar/2001-03-08a.pdf online] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060414075220/http://bio-math10.biology.kyushu-u.ac.jp/seminar/2001-03-08a.pdf |date=2006-04-14 }} (pdf file).</ref>

==Name==
The species was first scientifically described by Linnaeus in ''Species Plantarum'' in 1753. Its [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] ''lusitanica'' means "of Lusitania", referring to the Roman name for Portugal.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.instanthedge.com/portuguese-laurel/|title = Portuguese Laurel Hedge}}</ref>

==Subspecies==
Three [[subspecies]] are accepted:<ref name=powo/>
* '''''Prunus lusitanica'' subsp. ''lusitanica'''''. [[Iberian Peninsula]], South-West [[France]], and north [[Morocco]].
* '''''Prunus lusitanica'' subsp. ''azorica''''' (Mouill.) Franco. [[Azores]].<ref name=uac>Note: common names for ''Prunus lusitanica azorica'' include Ginja, Gingeira-brava and Ginjeira-do-Mato. {{ cite web |url=http://www.horta.uac.pt/species/plantae/Prunus_lusitanica_azorica/Prunus_lusitanica_azorica.htm |title=Prunus lusitanica azorica |publisher=University of the Azores |date=January 15, 2009 |access-date=May 21, 2009}}</ref>
* '''''Prunus lusitanica'' subsp. ''hixa''''' (Willd.) Franco. [[Canary Islands]] and [[Madeira]].

==Cultivation==
''Prunus lusitanica'' is grown as an [[ornamental plant|ornamental shrub]] and is widely planted as a [[hedge]] and for screening in gardens and parks.  It is introduced and locally [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in the [[temperateness|temperate]] zone in northern France, Great Britain, Ireland, New Zealand, Western Canada- including the southern BC Mainland and Vancouver Island From Victoria Up Island through the Cowichan, Nanaimo and Parksville as well as the western United States in California, Oregon and Washington State.{{cn|date=December 2023}}

Similar to its relative ''[[Prunus laurocerasus]]'', ''P. lusitanica'' has been recognized by some botanists and land managers in both western Washington and Oregon as invasive. It is thought to have spread from cultivated areas into natural areas by birds who consume the fruit and then defecate the seeds away from the source plant.{{cn|date=December 2023}}

It has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Prunus lusitanica''|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/14003/Prunus-lusitanica/Details | access-date=23 February 2020}}</ref>

==Toxicity==
The leaves of ''Prunus lusitanica'' contain [[hydrogen cyanide]] and will release this into the environment if burnt<ref name=cyn1>{{ cite web |url=http://www.paghat.com/portuguallaurel.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030508004208/http://www.paghat.com/portuguallaurel.html |url-status=usurped |archive-date=May 8, 2003 |title=Paghat's Garden: ''Prunus lusitanica'' |date=January 18, 2005 |access-date=June 14, 2009}},</ref> or if crushed.<ref name=cyn2>{{ cite web |url=http://www.rsc.org/Education/EiC/issues/2008July/ExhibitionChemistry.asp |title=EiC July 2008 - Feature - Exhibition chemistry: Toxic Hydrogen Cyanide |date=July 2008 |access-date=June 14, 2009}}</ref> The fruit is somewhat edible if fully ripe, but if it is bitter then it has too much hydrogen cyanide and should not be eaten.<ref name=pfaf>Plants for a Future: [http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Prunus+lusitanica ''Prunus lusitanica'']</ref>
